name: Zane Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What fills a normal day on site?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead finishing joinery on school projects: doors, stairs, cupboards and the hall stage. My vocational trade certificate gave me a start, and years of fitting awkward rooms made me a better teacher to the apprentices. I like a door that closes without a shove.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is hard about it now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Between contracts the paid days can be patchy. Priya, my partner, does bookkeeping part-time; we have two children in school, a mortgage and about four months saved. I use AI now and then for a stair sum after a colleague showed me, but I still measure every rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the joinery team that an app can sort a little paperwork, but a school door still has to shut square. I use a chatbot now and then for a stair calculation, never as the final measurement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya and I have about four months saved, two school-age children and a mortgage. My pay is typical for a lead joiner, and there are some other sites nearby, so the family can manage if work continues as expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting the school hall doors and teaching the apprentice to check the hinge side with a level. I would use the same occasional AI calculation, then mark the timber by hand before cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The ordinary worry is whether the next building contract starts on time, not whether a chatbot takes my saw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check after a stair calculation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rise and run on the actual floor, twice. A formula can be right while the slab is out of level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the household budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Priya’s bookkeeping hours and my site wage cover the mortgage now, and we would leave the savings transfer at its present amount.

say: I would tell the crew **school doors** still need a joiner checking the frame.
I would treat an occasional **AI calculation** as a rough aid before measuring the timber.
think: Our **four-month reserve** and two wages keep present family costs manageable.
The next **building contract** is my ordinary worry, even without much AI change.
do: Keep fitting **school hall doors** and teaching hinge-side checks.
Continue occasional **AI stair sums** but measure the floor before cutting.
feel: **Calm** about the current job and household money.
S0.quote: A formula can be right while the slab is out of level.
fieldNote: He already uses AI occasionally, but his **trade check** remains physical measurement.
Typical pay, Priya’s wages and a moderate reserve support **current household income security**.

steps.text: Keep fitting school hall doors and checking measurements with the apprentice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say quicker buying could stop us waiting for hinges, but someone should check the order against the actual door schedule. I would ask our contractor to show the crew a working trial before changing how we order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The purchasing office may shrink, and a faster schedule could mean fewer paid days between school projects. I might lose some hours, though Priya’s wage and the savings give us a few months to find a nearby site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI ordering screen if it passes a trial on one school wing. I would compare its next order with the hinge list and my own count, then watch two rosters before agreeing to a shorter crew schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible gap in paid days, not frightened of the screen itself. The mortgage needs wages between projects as well as during them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the trial fail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the screen orders the right count but the wrong fire-door hinge. I would return to the old signed list until a supplier and site joiner can check the correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you cut spending immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We have a few months saved and no pay cut yet. I would wait for rosters before changing the children’s activities.

I would keep a **joiner sign-off** on every fire-door order.
think: A faster schedule could remove **paid days** between projects.
Priya’s **bookkeeping wage** and savings buy time, but not unlimited mortgage payments.
do: Learn the new **AI ordering screen** only after a successful school-wing trial.
Compare its **hinge order** with the door schedule and a manual count.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic lost hours between school jobs.
S1.quote: The mortgage needs wages between projects as well as during them.
fieldNote: His interest in AI depends on a **proven site trial**, matching steady adaptability.
He has a clear **paid-days risk** without inventing an immediate contractor layoff.

steps.text: Learn new AI ordering controls after a successful school-wing trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices thinking AI in 2028 can draw a school stair, but nobody has a capable robot fitting it until around 2031. A first trial should use dead equipment in an empty room, with workers able to stop the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect some joinery crews to shrink when the robots can fit doors and stairs. I could lose paid days while the mortgage and children’s costs continue, although our savings and some nearby builders give me choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking paid joinery shifts and ask the manager for a written robot trial and staffing plan. If two rosters cut my hours, I would apply only to posted local joinery jobs with a firm wage that covers the mortgage and Priya’s work travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have room to search, but I cannot tell my children a drawing will pay for their school shoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does dead equipment mean in the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot arm should be powered down while the crew marks the test area and practises stopping it. Only then should a qualified operator power it for the empty-room test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without a posted offer that pays enough after travel and keeps the children near school. There are some jobs within reach, so I would check those first.

I would start with **powered-down equipment** and a stop check before an empty-room robot trial.
think: I could lose **paid joinery days** when capable robots arrive.
Four months saved and **some local builders** give us a search window.
do: Ask for a **written robot staffing plan** before trials.
Apply to **posted local joinery jobs** after two reduced rosters only for mortgage-covering firm pay.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hours loss while keeping a local search plan.
S2.quote: I cannot tell my children a drawing will pay for their school shoes.
fieldNote: He distinguishes the **2028 planning date** from 2031 hands-on capability.

steps.text: Keep paid school joinery shifts while contractor work exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets us test a machine on a crooked stair, not just a flat factory floor. I would insist the robot be isolated while apprentices learn where its arm can reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 changes drawings first; robots reach fitting work around 2034. I will be fifty one and still need paid work, so a quality-check role could help if the contractor actually creates one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the joinery crew next year. If the contractor posts a paid stair-quality vacancy and funds the course with paid study hours, I would complete the training and apply; if not, I would keep my trade shifts rather than buy a speculative certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the later job, but five years is enough to learn a proven check. I would not put the family’s savings into a course without a posted wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn to check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot’s stair rise, fasteners and final handrail height. I would still make the apprentice measure the finished run with a tape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train on a live arm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would start with the arm isolated and the power off, then move to a supervised test after the safety check. I would want those hours paid.

say: I would demand **crooked-stair trials** before 2034 joinery robots work on occupied buildings.
I would keep apprentices clear of **powered robot arms** during initial training.
think: I still need **paid work** at fifty one when robots reach site fitting.
A posted **quality-check job** could protect wages if paid training accompanies it.
do: Keep **school joinery shifts** while paid work continues.
Complete **funded stair-check training** only with paid study time and a posted mortgage-covering vacancy.
feel: **Anxious** about later work, with a conditional training route.
S3.quote: I would not put the family’s savings into a course without a posted wage.
fieldNote: He moves beyond occasional AI use only for a **funded real role**.
Safety begins with **isolated equipment**, then supervised practice on a live arm during paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell apprentices that a decade is enough to learn a proper stair and earn a trade certificate before thinking AI in 2036. Capable fitting robots around 2039 should be tested, not waved through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty six when robots arrive and still need a wage. The four-month cushion will not fund a decade without work. Savings still give us time to plan if site jobs shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep school joinery work in 2026 and put an extra twenty from each monthly wage toward the mortgage only if Priya’s hours and the children’s costs remain covered. In the first year after 2036 I would review actual site hours before choosing training; if robots cut jobs in 2039 I would apply only to posted wage-covering joinery work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far date, not frightened today. The long warning matters only if we put real pay behind the family plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why twenty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That is what we could spare after bills on a good month. If Priya loses bookkeeping hours, I would keep the cash for the next mortgage payment instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I will still have a family mortgage in my fifties. I want to work in a trade, even if the tools change.

I would demand **real-site tests** before a robot takes joinery work.
think: I will need **paid site work** around 2039 despite a four-month cushion.
The current **mortgage** and children’s needs make wages the planning base.

feel: **Uneasy** about distant job risk while present work remains secure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots might reach school joinery in 2031 while I still need the mortgage wage. Paid quality training for a posted role, a safe powered-down trial and firm nearby vacancies would give me choices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a stair after the robot leaves. A child will use that handrail long after the demonstration team goes home.

headlineQuote: A child will use that handrail long after the demonstration team goes home.
portrait: **Zane**, 43, leads school joinery with a trade certificate, typical pay, four months saved and some nearby building work.
He and Priya support **two school-age children** and a mortgage, so paid days between projects matter.
He uses **AI occasionally** once proven, values apprenticeships and insists robot training begin with isolated equipment.
The **2028 case** worries him because 2031 robots could reduce joinery hours while the mortgage continues.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut paid school joinery days once capable robots reach sites in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training for a **posted quality role**, safe trials and firm nearby work would help.
